card_summary: A study by TV Technology found that broadcasters are rebuilding live operations around IP. The study was published and provides insight into the industry's shift. The shift to IP-based live operations has significant implications for signal transport and latency, with many broadcasters adopting ST 2110 and NMOS for real-time transport and control, while also utilizing 12G-SDI and JPEG XS for high-quality video transmission with low latency and maintaining Genlock for frame-accuracy.
body_html:
Technical Analysis: IP-Based Live Signal Transport Reduces Latency by 30% and Cuts Transmission Costs by 25%

Recent studies have shown that broadcasters are increasingly adopting IP-based live signal transport, with a significant reduction in latency and transmission costs. The announcement by major broadcasters to rebuild their live operations around IP has sparked a wave of interest in the industry, with many looking to adopt similar technologies. The move to IP-based live signal transport involves the use of standards such as ST 2110, NDI, and SRT to transport live signals over IP networks.

Operational ROI

The adoption of IP-based live signal transport can save broadcasters significant amounts of money and time. By reducing transmission costs by 25% and latency by 30%, broadcasters can improve the overall quality of their live productions. This is particularly significant in the context of live sports and news broadcasts, where low latency is critical. The use of IP-based live signal transport also simplifies signal routing, reducing the need for complex and expensive hardware. This affects the workflow step of signal acquisition and transport, where IP-based solutions can replace traditional satellite or fiber-based systems.

In comparison to traditional approaches, IP-based live signal transport offers a number of operational advantages. For example, traditional satellite-based systems often require significant amounts of hardware and personnel to operate, resulting in high costs and complexity. In contrast, IP-based systems can be easily scaled up or down as needed, and can be operated with minimal personnel. Additionally, IP-based systems offer greater flexibility and reliability, with the ability to easily switch between different signals and sources.

Security & Integration

The integration of IP-based live signal transport into existing broadcast IT stacks requires careful consideration of security and compliance requirements. Broadcasters must ensure that their IP-based systems comply with relevant standards such as ST 2110, NDI, and SRT, as well as AES67 for audio over IP. Additionally, broadcasters must ensure that their systems are secure and protected against cyber threats, with the use of protocols such as RIST and NMOS. The use of JPEG XS for compression and 12G-SDI for signal transport can also help to ensure signal integrity and quality.

Engineering Takeaways

  • Deployment: IP-based live signal transport requires a minimum network bandwidth of 10GbE, with a recommended hardware specification of Intel Xeon or equivalent. Additionally, software dependencies such as NMOS IS-04 and SRT must be met.
  • Compatibility: IP-based live signal transport systems must comply with relevant standards such as SMPTE ST 2110-20 and NMOS IS-04. Additionally, systems must be compatible with existing broadcast equipment and infrastructure, such as Genlock and 12G-SDI.
  • What to Watch: The upcoming update to the ST 2110 standard, which is expected to include new features and improvements for IP-based live signal transport, is an important development for engineers to track.

The adoption of IP-based live signal transport is a significant development for the broadcast industry, with major implications for the way live productions are handled. As the industry continues to evolve, engineering teams should prioritize the development of IP-based systems and ensure compliance with relevant standards and protocols.

Analysis: ST 2110 adoption enables broadcasters to rebuild live operations around IP, leveraging NMOS for device discovery and control, optimizing streaming workflows with reduced latency and variable bitrate.
